offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which may extend to three years and shall also be liable to fine
physical_harm: No injuries or death caused directly by the appellant, but the deceased was described as 'well nourished' and had her last meal within six hours
number_of_offences: Two offences/counts charged, one finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted that the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant subjected the deceased to cruelty of the nature described in the Explanation to Section 498A, IPC. The Court also noted that the post mortem report showed the deceased was well nourished and not subjected to severe beating.
witness_credibility: The Court assessed the credibility of PW-1 and PW-4, noting that their depositions suggested the deceased was sad due to her daughter being born and her husband's first wife having a son, which may have led to her suicide. However, the Court found that such circumstances alone do not constitute cruelty within the meaning of the Explanation to Section 498A, IPC.
bail_history: Bail bonds executed by the appellant be discharged
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 15.07.1988; Trial judgment: 09.01.1991; High Court decision: 03.12.2003; Supreme Court decision: 08.02.2013
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Anagha Desai, Shashant Pareek, Satyajit A. Desai, C Venkateswara Rao Anumolu; Counsel for the State: Shankar Chillagre, Asha Gopalan Nair
investigation_status: FIR registered under Sections 306 and 498A of the IPC; charge-sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted appellant of offences punishable under Sections 306 and 498-A/PC; High Court: Maintained conviction of appellant; Supreme Court: Set aside the conviction and sentence of the appellant
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant subjected the deceased to cruelty, leading to her suicide, and relied on the evidence of PW-1 and PW-4, as well as the FIR and the written undertakings (Exts. 47 and 48) to establish the cruelty and abetment of suicide.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the appellant subjected the deceased to cruelty of the nature described in the Explanation to Section 498A, IPC. They emphasized that the written undertakings (Exts. 47 and 48) did not establish actual cruelty, and the post-mortem report showed no severe injuries or denial of food.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that for the presumption under Section 113A of the Evidence Act to be attracted, there must be evidence of cruelty of the nature described in the Explanation to Section 498A, IPC.
precedent_relied_upon: State of West Bengal v. Ori/la Jaiswal & Anr. (1994) 1 SCC 73
